slides.title: What is a Computing System?
slides.body:
Introduction
 A computing system is a combination of hardware and software that work together to perform tasks, such as processing data, running applications, and managing resources
Hardware
Software
slides.notes: have you ever wondered what makes a computer actually work? A computing system is a combination of hardware and software working together. While hardware provides the physical components, software gives them instructions to perform tasks like processing data and running applications.

slides.title: What is a Computing System?
slides.body:
Hardware & Software 
Hardware
Software
The physical components of a computer 
Programs and instructions that control hardware
slides.notes: Next, let's understand these two components. Hardware refers to the physical parts of a computer that we can see and touch, while software consists of the programs and instructions that tell the hardware what to do. Both are essential for a computing system to function properly.

slides.title: Overview of Computer Hardware
slides.body: Overview of Computer Hardware
slides.notes: Now we will understand about the Overview of Computer Hardware

slides.title: Introduction to Computer Hardware
slides.body:
Computer Hardware
External components
Internal components
slides.notes: Computer hardware can be broadly classified into internal and external components.Internal components, like the processor and memory, are placed inside the computer and perform core operations. External components, such as the monitor, keyboard, and mouse, allow us to interact with the computer.

slides.title: Computer Hardware
slides.body:
Internal Components
Component parts that are found inside the computer
Motherboard
Hard Disk , RAM & CPU
Graphics Card (GPU)
Registers
BIOS
UEFI etc.
slides.notes: let's look at the internal components of a computer. These are the parts located inside the system that perform essential operations.Some common examples include the motherboard, CPU, RAM, hard disk, graphics card, registers, and firmware like BIOS and UEFI, each playing a specific role in the computer's functioning.

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body:
MotherBoard
The motherboard is the computer's central communications backbone connectivity point through which all components and external components connect
slides.notes: Next, have you ever wondered what connects all the components inside a computer? That's the role of the motherboard. It acts as the main circuit board, allowing internal and external components to communicate and work together seamlessly.

slides.title: Memory
slides.body:
Hard Drive
Non-volatile storage
Responsible for storing permanent and temporary data
SSD (Solid-state drives) are much faster than regular HDDs (Hard-disk drives)
slides.notes: Moving on, the hard drive is the computer's non-volatile storage, which means it retains data even when the power is turned off. It stores the operating system, applications, and user files. Today, SSDs(Solid-state drives) are preferred over HDDs(Hard-disk drives) because they provide much faster data access and better performance.

slides.title: Memory
slides.body:
RAM is volatile memory
Data remains in RAM if the computer is on, but it's lost when the computer is turned off
RAM is much faster to read and write than other types of storage
RAM
RAM
slides.notes: Next, let's understand RAM, or Random Access Memory. It is volatile memory, meaning it stores data only while the computer is powered on. Since RAM is much faster than permanent storage, it temporarily holds the data and programs that the CPU is currently using.

slides.title: Memory
slides.body: RAM vs Hard Drive
slides.notes: Manufacturing of the ram is expensive. 8GB - 1TB - 4000/-
tables: Hard drive is a nonvolatile memory

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body:
Central Processing Unit (CPU)
The CPU (Central Processing Unit or processor) is responsible for processing all information from programs
It processes many instructions from different programs every second
slides.notes: Moving on, the CPU, or Central Processing Unit, is often called the brain of the computer. It executes instructions from programs, performs calculations, and processes millions of instructions every second to keep the system running smoothly.

slides.title: Memory
slides.body:
Registers
Registers are a type of computer memory used to quickly accept, store, and transfer data and instructions that are being used immediately by the CPU
slides.notes: Next, have you ever wondered where the CPU keeps the data it needs instantly? That's the role of registers. They are the fastest type of memory, used to temporarily store data and instructions that the CPU is currently processing.

slides.title: CPU
slides.body:
CPU Instruction Set
Programs on computer are broken down into very small and simple instructions
Add two numbers
Load value from Memory Location
Store Value to Memory Location
slides.notes: Moving on, have you ever wondered how the CPU understands a program? Every program is broken down into small, simple instructions, such as adding two numbers, loading data from memory, or storing data back into memory. The CPU executes these instructions one by one.

slides.title: CPU
slides.body:
CPU Clock Speed
The clock speed measures the number of cycles CPU can execute per second
Measured in gigahertz (GHz)
1 GHz = 1 Billion clock cycles per second 
A higher clock speed means a faster CPU
slides.notes: Next, what determines how fast a CPU works? It's the clock speed, which indicates how many processing cycles the CPU performs every second. It is measured in gigahertz (GHz), where 1 GHz equals one billion clock cycles per second. Generally, a higher clock speed means the CPU can execute instructions faster.

slides.title: CPU
slides.body:
CPU Cores
A core is an individual processing unit inside the CPU.
Each core can execute instructions independently — like a small CPU inside the main CPU
Multiple cores may work together to perform parallel operations
slides.notes:
Moving on, let's understand what a CPU core is. 
A core is an individual processing unit inside the CPU, and each core can execute instructions independently on its own. 
With multiple cores, the CPU can perform multiple tasks in parallel, improving overall performance and efficiency.

slides.title: CPU
slides.body:
Running Applications
Running applications are loaded into RAM
Executes the instruction
 Data required for current computation loaded to register
Applications
Registers
Registers
slides.notes:
Next, let's see what happens when you run an application. It is first loaded from storage into RAM. 
The data and instructions needed immediately are then moved to the CPU registers, and finally, the CPU executes those instructions to run the application.

slides.title: CPU Architecture
slides.body:
32-bit and 64-bit Systems
A 32-bit processor includes a 32-bit register, which can store 232 values
Can support upto 4 GB RAM
A 64-bit processor includes a 64-bit register, which can store 264
Can support up to billions of GB of RAM
slides.notes: Moving on, the difference between 32-bit and 64-bit systems lies in the size of their registers. A 32-bit processor can store 2³² values and supports up to 4 GB of RAM, whereas a 64-bit processor can store 2⁶⁴ values and supports much larger amounts of RAM, making it ideal for modern systems.

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body:
Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)
Specialized processor designed to deal with specific types of instructions efficiently
3D Rendering
Games
Deep Learning
slides.notes:
Next, let's look at the Graphics Processing Unit, or GPU. 
It is a specialized processor designed to handle tasks that involve large-scale parallel computations efficiently, such as 3D rendering, gaming, and deep learning applications.

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body: CPU vs GPU
slides.notes: Moving on, let's compare the CPU and GPU. A CPU is designed to handle a wide variety of tasks and typically has a few powerful cores. In contrast, a GPU has thousands of smaller cores, making it highly efficient at performing many operations in parallel, such as graphics processing and AI workloads.
tables: A CPU can perform a variety of different instructions
GPU can perform a specialized set of instructions
Has 1000s of Cores, good at parallelization

slides.title: Memory
slides.body:
Data Access Time
Data Access Time is the amount of time a storage device (like registers, RAM, hard disk) takes to locate and deliver the requested data to the CPU
slides.notes: Moving on, data access time refers to how quickly a storage device(like registers, RAM, hard disk) can retrieve the required data and make it available to the CPU.Registers are the fastest, with an access time of less than 2 nanoseconds and transfer speeds of over 100 GB/s. RAM takes around 50–100 nanoseconds with speeds of 25–50 GB/s, while hard disks are much slower, taking 5–10 milliseconds and transferring data at around 100–250 MB/s.

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body:
BIOS
Basic Input/Output System (BIOS) 
Initializes the hardware and gets our operating system up and running
Power on
POST
Beep Code
Error
Tests essential hardware 
Locates & Start OS
Applies Hardware specific settings
slides.notes: Moving on, have you ever wondered what happens the moment you power on a computer? The BIOS, or Basic Input/Output System, is the first software that runs. It checks whether the essential hardware is working through POST, reports any issues using beep codes, applies the required hardware settings, and finally locates and starts the operating system.

slides.title: Hardware Internal Components
slides.body:
UEFI
UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is similar to BIOS
Support for latest hardware
Secure Boot
Faster Boot
slides.notes: Next, UEFI, or Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, is the modern replacement for BIOS.It provides better support for newer hardware, offers security features like Secure Boot, and enables the system to boot faster than traditional BIOS.

slides.title: Computer Hardware
slides.body:
External Components
External hardware components, or peripherals, are input/output devices
Keyboard & Mouse
Monitors & Speakers 
USB Drives
Web Cam
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at external components, also known as peripherals. These are devices connected to the computer that help us provide input or receive output. Common examples include the keyboard, mouse, monitor, speakers, USB drives, and webcam.

slides.title: Hardware External Components Interfaces
slides.body:
Ports
Connectors or Ports that allow us to plug in different external components to computer to enhance its capabilities
slides.notes: Next, how do we connect external devices to a computer? That's where ports come in. They act as connection points, allowing peripherals such as USB drives, keyboards, monitors, and other devices to communicate with the computer and extend its functionality.

slides.title: Hardware External Components Interfaces
slides.body:
Display and Audio Ports
DVI Port
VGA Port
Video Ports
Display Port
HDMI Port
Video & Audio Ports
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at some common display and audio ports. DVI and VGA are primarily used to transmit video signals, while Display Port and HDMI can carry both video and audio, making them the preferred choice for connecting modern monitors and TVs.

slides.title: Ports
slides.body: USB Port
slides.notes: Next, one of the most commonly used ports is the USB port.Over time, USB has evolved into different types, including Type-A, Type-C, Mini USB, and Micro USB, each designed for specific devices and use cases.

slides.title: Ports
slides.body:
USB Port
USB (Universal Serial Bus) Port
Designed to standardize many peripheral connections
Audio
Video
Data Transfer 
Power
slides.notes: USB, or Universal Serial Bus, was introduced to provide a standard way of connecting peripherals. Besides transferring data, USB ports can also carry power, audio, and even video, making them one of the most versatile ports available today.

slides.title: Hardware & Software
slides.body:
Understanding Software 
Software
Includes Operating System (OS) (Windows, Linux) and Applications (Word, Chrome, Games)
Operating systems
Applications
Windows
Linux
Word
Chrome
Games
slides.notes:
So, we've explored the hardware components of a computer. Now, let's understand software, which is broadly classified into operating systems and applications. The operating system, such as Windows or Linux, manages the hardware,
while applications like Word, Chrome, and games help users perform specific tasks.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body: Operating System
slides.notes: Moving on , next we will be learning about the Operating System .

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
Hardware and Software
Now that we understand hardware and software, let’s see an example of how they work together in a real-life scenario
slides.notes: Since, we've understood what hardware and software are individually. Let's see how they work together in a real-world scenario to understand the role of the operating system in connecting the two.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
Example
Customers place orders with the waiter
Waiter passes the order to the chef
Chef cooks and gives it back to the waiter
Waiter serves the food to the customer
slides.notes: let's understand this with a simple restaurant example. The customer places an order with the waiter, who communicates it to the chef. Once the food is prepared, the waiter brings it back to the customer. In the same way, we'll see how the operating system acts as an intermediary between applications and the computer's hardware.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
What Happens Without Coordination?
What happens if the chef had to take orders from every customer directly?
slides.notes: Next, what do you think would happen if every customer went directly to the chef instead of placing orders through the waiter? It would create confusion, delays, and make it difficult to manage multiple orders efficiently.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
Waiter as a Coordinator
Someone is needed to coordinate orders, manage the kitchen, and serve customers efficiently
Waiter
Set up the dining area 
Coordinate orders
Serve customers
slides.notes: to avoid this confusion, we need someone to coordinate everything. In a restaurant, that's the waiter. The waiter takes orders, coordinates with the kitchen, serves customers, and ensures everything runs smoothly and efficiently.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
OS as a Coordinator
Similarly, a computer needs a manager to coordinate between users, applications, and hardware, that manager is the Operating System (OS)
slides.notes: Now, just as a waiter coordinates everything in a restaurant, a computer also needs a coordinator. That's the Operating System, which acts as a bridge between the user, applications, and hardware, ensuring they work together efficiently.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
What is an Operating System?
An operating system (OS) is a software that acts as an interface between a computer's hardware and the user, managing all its resources and basic operations
Operating System
Hardware resources
Software resources
Manages
slides.notes: So lets define an Operating SystemIt is a software that acts as an interface between the user and the computer's hardware.—> It manages both hardware and software resources, ensuring that programs run efficiently and the system operates smoothly.

slides.title: What is an Operating System?
slides.body:
How the Operating System works ?
Users
Application
Operating System
Hardware
CPU
I/O
RAM
slides.notes: let's see how an Operating System works. Users interact with applications, and those applications communicate with the Operating System. The OS then manages the hardware resources, such as the CPU, memory, and input/output devices, and returns the results back to the application and the user.

slides.title: Introduction to OS
slides.body:
Examples of Operating System
Operating System
Desktop Operating Systems
Windows
Linux
Mac OS
Chrome OS
Mobile Operating Systems
Android
IOS
slides.notes: Finally, there are different operating systems designed for different devices. Desktop operating systems include Windows, Linux, macOS, and ChromeOS, while mobile operating systems include Android and iOS. Although they run on different devices, they all perform the same core role of managing hardware and software resources.

slides.title: Examples of Operating System
slides.body:
Desktop Operating Systems
Windows
Most widely used desktop OS globally
Known for extensive software compatibility
Common in business and personal computing
slides.notes: Moving on, let's start with Windows, the most widely used desktop operating system. It is known for its broad software compatibility and is commonly used in homes, businesses, and educational institutions around the world.

slides.title: Examples of Operating System
slides.body:
Desktop Operating Systems
macOS
Popular for creative and design work
Known for stability, security, and ease of use
slides.notes: Next, let's look at macOS, Apple's desktop operating system. It is widely preferred for creative and design-related work and is well known for its stability, security, and user-friendly experience.

slides.title: Examples of Operating System
slides.body:
Desktop Operating Systems
Linux
Open-source OS with multiple distributions (Ubuntu, Fedora, etc.)
Widely used on servers and by developers
Growing popularity for desktop use
slides.notes:
Moving on, Linux is an open-source operating system available in multiple distributions, 
such as Ubuntu and Fedora. It is widely used on servers and by developers, and its popularity as a desktop operating system continues to grow.

slides.title: Examples of Operating System
slides.body:
Mobile Operating Systems
Android 
Linux-based, open-source
Designed for touch-based, mobile devices
iOS 
Apple's mobile OS  for iPhone/iPad
Known for security and smooth performance
slides.notes: Finally, let's look at the two most popular mobile operating systems. Android is a Linux-based, open-source operating system designed for touchscreen devices. iOS, on the other hand, is Apple's operating system for iPhones and iPads, known for its strong security and smooth performance.

slides.title: Types of Software
slides.body: Types of Software
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Types of Software

slides.title: Software
slides.body:
Where Does an Operating System Belong?
Is an operating system the only software a computer needs?
slides.notes: Moving on, we've learned about the operating system, but is it the only software a computer needs? Not really. Let's understand where the operating system fits among the different types of software used in a computer system.

slides.title: Software
slides.body:
Types of Software
Computers use different types of software for different purposes
Types of Software
System Software
Application Software
Controls how the computer operates
Helps users perform specific tasks
slides.notes: Next, software can be broadly classified into two types: system software and application software. System software manages and controls the computer's operations, while application software helps users perform specific tasks, such as browsing the internet, editing documents, or playing games.

slides.title: Types of Software
slides.body:
System Software
What is a System Software?
Software that manages computer hardware
Provides a platform for applications to run
slides.notes: Moving on, what exactly is system software? It is the software responsible for managing the computer's hardware and providing a platform on which application software can run efficiently.

slides.title: System Software
slides.body:
Components of System Software
Operating System
The main controller (Windows, Linux, MacOS)
Device Drivers
Enable communication with hardware devices (printer drivers, graphics drivers)
Utility Programs
System maintenance tools (antivirus, disk cleanup, file managers)
Key Point
An Operating System is the most important type of system software!
slides.notes: Next, system software consists of several components. 1. The Operating System acts as the main controller,  2.  device drivers enable communication with hardware devices, 3 and utility programs help maintain and optimize the system. Among these, the Operating System is the most important system software.

slides.title: Types of Software
slides.body:
Application Software
Programs designed to help users perform specific tasks
Application Software
slides.notes: Finally, application software is designed to help users perform specific tasks.Depending on the purpose, it can include web browsers, media applications, games, and development tools. Unlike system software, these programs are used directly by users to accomplish everyday activities.

slides.title: OS Components
slides.body: OS Components
slides.notes: Next we will be learning about the OS Components

slides.title: Introduction to Operating System
slides.body:
Components of OS
Hardware
Operating System
slides.notes: Moving on, let's understand the main components of an Operating System. Applications run in the user space, while the kernel acts as the core of the OS. The kernel manages processes, memory, files, and I/O, while acting as a bridge between applications and the hardware.

slides.title: Introduction to Operating System
slides.body:
User Space
User space is everything outside the kernel
Programs we interact with directly are part of User Space
Text Editors, Music Players, User Interfaces, etc
slides.notes:
Next, let's understand User Space. It is the part of the system where user applications run. 
These are the programs we interact with directly, such as text editors, music players, and the user interface, while the operating system manages their access to hardware.

slides.title: Introduction to Operating System
slides.body:
OS Kernel
Kernel is the core component of OS 
Interacts directly with hardware
Manages the hardware resources 
Hardware
slides.notes: Next, the kernel is responsible for the core operations of the operating system. It communicates directly with the hardware and manages processes, memory, files, and input/output devices, ensuring that applications can use hardware safely and efficiently.

slides.title: Operating System
slides.body: Linux Kernel
slides.notes:
Moving on, have you ever wondered what Linux actually is? At its core, Linux is a free and open-source kernel developed by Linus Torvalds. 
Different operating systems built using the Linux kernel are called Linux distributions, or simply Linux distros.

slides.title: From Components to Functions
slides.body:
How Components Enable OS Functions
Components = The parts that make up the OS
Functions = What these parts actually do
Key Point
Components work together to perform functions
slides.notes: Next, we've understood the components of an operating system. But what do these components actually do? The components work together to perform different functions, allowing the operating system to manage the computer efficiently.

slides.title: From Components to Functions
slides.body:
How Components Enable OS Functions
Kernel
Process Manager
Memory Manager
File Systems
I/O System
Components
Functions
Resource management
Running Programs
Allocating RAM
Organizing Data
Device control
Security Module
Security & Protection
slides.notes: let's connect the components we've learned with the functions they perform. The kernel manages system resources, the process manager runs programs, the memory manager allocates RAM, the file system organizes data, the I/O system controls devices, and the security module protects the system. Together, these components enable the operating system to function efficiently.
